newsitem.title: SPAIN: EU pact greeted with relief in Spanish newspapers.
newsitem.headline: EU pact greeted with relief in Spanish newspapers.

text.p: Spanish newspapers welcomed with relief on Tuesday a European Union summit agreement in Amsterdam to affirm a key budget stability pact by adding a complementary jobs accord.

Editorials and reports in most major Spanish newspapers said Europe's monetary union now seemed solidly on track and at the same time, steps were being taken to alleviate joblessness, one of the biggest worries for Spaniards.

"The Amsterdam summit has closed the Pandora's Box that French President Jacques Chirac opened the day he decided to move elections in his country forward," financial daily Negocios said. "The crisis, at least, has been overcome and the markets can now breathe easily until the next scare."

Negocios said there was now room for the Bank of Spain to lower interest rates at its regular repurchase tender on June 24, a decision that had been put off ahead of the Amsterdam summit despite economic indicators that there was room to cut.
Spain's leading daily El Pais said the deal on jobs was just a starting point in the fight against unemployment.

"The road toward the euro has again straightened itself out, and, from now, European construction will pay more attention to the main worry of almost all citizens: employment," an El Pais editorial said. "The accord yesterday was not a goal score, but the kickoff for a common fight against unemployment."
El Pais said that the essential elements of that fight would remain in the hands of national governments, which is what Spain wanted, along with Germany and Britain.
Calling it a typical European Union manoeuvre, major daily El Mundo lamented the delay in concrete steps on joblessness and said the deal was vague and spineless.
But the newspaper said in an editorial that at least European Union leaders were paying some attention to social issues as they renegotiated the treaty on Europe.
"Thanks to the demands laid on by Paris during a stormy week that had the stock markets reeling, the social question will start to count in the European Union," El Mundo said.

Conservative daily ABC said the deal was good for Spain because there was no money figure attached to the agreement to coordinate policies in the fight to find jobs for Europe's 18 million unemployed.
ABC said in an editorial that Spain could not afford any diversion to jobs of the European cohesion fund money it gets for infrastructure development.
